overview.title: 📖 Overview: Candelabra, Lamps, and the Limits of Muktzeh
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 46a–46b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין מוּקְצֶה לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אֶלָּא שֶׁמֶן שֶׁבַּנֵּר בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהוּא דּוֹלֵק
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through why a candelabrum made of separable joints may not be moved — concern that it will fall apart and be reassembled, itself a Torah-level act of construction — and extends this by rabbinic decree even to a small candelabrum merely decorated with grooves that resemble joints. A string of anecdotes shows individual Sages moving or refusing to move a lamp depending on whose locale they were in, out of deference to Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara then debates whether a naphtha lamp, unlike an oil lamp, may be moved, with Rav Avya defending the lenient view to Rava using the concept of 'the legal status of a vessel' (torat keli). The daf closes by resolving an apparent contradiction: Rabbi Shimon permits leftover lamp oil but seems to treat an unexpectedly blemished firstborn animal as muktzeh.

slides.title: 🔧 A Candelabrum of Joints: Building by Accident
slides.subtitle: Why moving it risks an unintended act of construction

steps.content: 1️⃣ Abaye: the concern is a candelabrum made of actual removable joints — it might fall apart while being moved, and reassembling it is prohibited construction
2️⃣ Question: if so, why does Reish Lakish permit moving it at all?
3️⃣ Resolved: 'joints' really means grooves that merely resemble joints for decoration — nothing will actually fall apart
4️⃣ Rule: a candelabrum with real joints — large or small — may never be moved; a large grooved one is forbidden too, by rabbinic decree, so people won't confuse it with the jointed kind

callout.label: Where they disagree:
callout.text: Only for a small, merely-grooved candelabrum: Rabbi Yochanan decrees against it (fearing confusion with the large kind), while Reish Lakish permits it, since a small candelabrum is not typically made of true joints.

slides.title: 🕎 Testing Rabbi Yochanan's Consistency
slides.subtitle: Does he really follow Rabbi Yehuda's stricter view on muktzeh?
rows: Permits pulling a wagon once no money is on it, even if money sat there at twilight — sounds like Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Zeira: read the mishna as if no money was ever there during twilight at all
Rebbi ruled on a candelabrum 'like Rabbi Shimon ruled on a lamp' — but which way?

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: Rabbi Yochanan is known to rule by the unattributed mishna — so if that mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, his own contrary rulings need explaining.

slides.title: 🕯️ Moving a Lamp — Depending on Whose House You're In
slides.subtitle: A string of anecdotes about deference, not disagreement

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Rav Malkiya moved a lamp at Rabbi Simlai's house and was scolded; Rabbi Yosei HaGlili did the same at Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Chanina's and was scolded too.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But Rabbi Abbahu moved a lamp at Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's place, and refrained from doing so at Rabbi Yochanan's place!

lines.speaker: Question
lines.text: Whichever way he personally rules, shouldn't he act consistently everywhere?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Rabbi Abbahu actually held like Rabbi Shimon (lenient) throughout — but out of honor for Rabbi Yochanan, he did not act against his host's ruling in his own place.

slides.title: 🛢️ May a Naphtha Lamp Be Moved?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yehuda's stricter view against Rabba and Rav Yosef, tested by Rav Avya

nodes.content: ⚖️ Rav Yehuda: an extinguished oil lamp may be moved; a naphtha lamp may not — its smell is unpleasant, so it has no other use
💡 Rabba and Rav Yosef: even a naphtha lamp may be moved, since it is still suitable to cover another vessel
❓ Rava challenges Rav Avya: if 'suitable to cover a vessel' is enough, then pebbles in the yard should also be movable for the same reason!
✅ Rav Avya answers: a lamp already carries 'the legal status of a vessel' (torat keli), so a secondary use suffices to permit it; raw pebbles have no such status to begin with

callout.label: Supporting proof:
callout.text: A baraita teaches that bracelets, nose-rings, and rings may be moved in a courtyard precisely because 'the legal status of a vessel applies to them' — Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak thanks God that Rava did not embarrass Rav Avya.

slides.title: 🐑 Reconciling Two Rulings of Rabbi Shimon
slides.subtitle: Leftover lamp oil is permitted, but a blemished firstborn seems forbidden — why?

boxes.title: Leftover Lamp Oil
items: A person sits and anticipates exactly when the lamp will go out
The remaining oil is expected in advance

boxes.title: A Firstborn's Blemish
items: Rabbi Shimon: if the blemish wasn't visible before the Festival, the animal is 'not among the prepared'
Full of uncertainty: will a blemish appear? Will it be permanent? Will a Sage examine it?
Because it's so unexpected, it never entered anyone's mind — hence set aside

callout.label: Rabba's resolution:
callout.text: The cases differ in predictability, not principle — expected leftover oil is never truly set aside, while a wholly unanticipated blemish is. A parallel question about nullifying vows on Shabbat is resolved the same way.

summary.principle: Even Rabbi Shimon's lenient view of muktzeh has real boundaries: an object stays permitted only when its future use was genuinely anticipated, and the Sages layer rabbinic decrees onto cases that merely resemble a forbidden one, to prevent confusion.

flowSteps.content: 🔧 A jointed candelabrum risks accidental construction; decree extends even to look-alike grooves
🕯️ Sages defer to their host's ruling on moving a lamp, even against their own view

columns.content: 🛢️ A naphtha lamp keeps 'vessel status,' unlike raw pebbles
🐑 Predictable leftover oil is not set aside; an unforeseen blemish is

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an item is set aside only when its future use was neither anticipated nor already established as a vessel

quiz.q: Why is it forbidden to move a candelabrum made of actual removable joints on Shabbat?
o: It is too heavy
It might fall apart while being moved, and reassembling it constitutes prohibited construction
It is disrespectful to the household
Candelabra are always forbidden
quiz.e: Abaye explains the concern is that the candelabrum could come apart into its component pieces during moving, and reassembling it would be a Torah-level act of building.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara forbid moving even a large candelabrum that merely has decorative grooves (not real joints)?
o: Large candelabra are always heavier
By rabbinic decree, since it could be mistaken for a genuinely jointed candelabrum
It has no practical use
It belongs to a different category entirely
quiz.e: Because large candelabra are commonly made of real joints, a rabbinic decree forbids even a large grooved one, out of concern people would mistake it for the jointed type.

quiz.q: Why did Rabbi Abbahu move a lamp at Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's home but not at Rabbi Yochanan's home?
o: He held different opinions in each place
He personally held like the lenient Rabbi Shimon throughout, but deferred to Rabbi Yochanan's stricter ruling out of respect when in his place
Rabbi Yochanan's house had no lamps
It was a scribal error
quiz.e: The Gemara explains Rabbi Abbahu consistently held like Rabbi Shimon (lenient), but out of honor for Rabbi Yochanan he did not act against his host's own ruling in his locale.

quiz.q: According to Rav Avya, why may a naphtha lamp be moved even though it is unpleasant to be near, while ordinary pebbles suitable for covering a vessel may not?
o: Naphtha lamps are lighter than pebbles
A lamp already carries the legal status of a vessel (torat keli), so a secondary use suffices to keep it movable; raw pebbles never had that status
Pebbles are always forbidden regardless of use
There is no real difference between them
quiz.e: Rav Avya distinguishes: an item that is already a recognized vessel remains movable if it has any secondary use, but raw material like pebbles needs to be specifically designated before Shabbat to become movable.

quiz.q: How does Rabba resolve the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Shimon permitting leftover lamp oil but treating an unexpectedly blemished firstborn animal as set aside?
o: He says Rabbi Shimon contradicts himself
A person predictably anticipates exactly when a lamp will go out, but does not anticipate an unpredictable, uncertain blemish appearing on an animal
Blemished animals are never usable on Shabbat regardless
Oil and animals follow completely unrelated rules with no comparison possible
quiz.e: Rabba explains the difference is predictability: one sits and expects the lamp's oil to run out, but a blemish appearing, being permanent, and being examined by a Sage are all uncertain, so it was never anticipated.
